questions.prompt: In 1977, Rod Johnstone built the very first J/24 in his garage, launching the legendary J/Boats brand. What was the name of this famous first hull?

options.text: Windward
options.feedback: "Windward" is a generic sailing term for the direction the wind is blowing from, not the name of the first J/24.

options.text: Ragtime
options.feedback: Spot on! Rod Johnstone built "Ragtime" in his Stonington, Connecticut garage. It dominated local racing, leading to the mass production of the J/24.

options.text: Intrepid
options.feedback: "Intrepid" was a famous 12-meter yacht that won the America's Cup twice, but it was not a J/Boat.

options.text: Black Magic
options.feedback: "Black Magic" (NZL 32) is the legendary boat that won the America's Cup for New Zealand in 1995, not a 24-foot garage build!

questions.prompt: Introduced in 1991, the J/105 revolutionized the sailing world. What major design innovation made the J/105 stand out from traditional keelboats of its time?

options.text: It was the first production boat built entirely of carbon fiber.
options.feedback: In 1991, carbon fiber was still far too expensive for mass-produced recreational keelboats; the J/105 hull is fiberglass.

options.text: It featured a completely unstayed mast.
options.feedback: The J/105 has a traditional stayed rig (with shrouds and stays). Unstayed masts are more common on boats like the Nonsuch.

options.text: It was the first modern keelboat to feature a retractable bowsprit and an asymmetric spinnaker.
options.feedback: Exactly! The J/105 changed the game by introducing the retractable bowsprit and asymmetric spinnaker to a production keelboat, making downwind sailing faster and easier with a smaller crew.

options.text: It utilized a canting keel for offshore racing.
options.feedback: Canting keels swing side-to-side and are used on extreme offshore racers like IMOCA 60s, whereas the J/105 has a standard fixed fin keel.

questions.prompt: The E-Scow is a lightning-fast, flat-bottomed boat that has been raced on inland lakes for a century. Roughly when was the E-Scow officially recognized as a national class?

options.feedback: Correct! The E-Scow has an incredible legacy and was recognized as a national class in 1923. Early versions were built of wood and heavily over-canvased.
1945 is the year Melges Boat Works was founded (a major builder of scows), but the E-Scow class already existed before then.
This date is much too late! The E-Scow is a true classic design with over 100 years of racing history.

questions.prompt: Melges Performance Sailboats has been a staple of high-performance racing for decades. Who originally founded the company in Zenda, Wisconsin?

options.text: Buddy Melges
options.feedback: Buddy Melges is Harry's son. Buddy became a sailing legend (winning Olympic medals and the America's Cup), but his father started the business.

options.text: Johnstone Melges
options.feedback: This is a trick answer combining the Johnstone family (J/Boats) with the Melges family!

options.text: Gary Jobson
options.feedback: Gary Jobson is a famous American sailor, tactician, and sailing commentator, but he did not found Melges.

options.text: Harry Melges Sr.
options.feedback: That's right! Harry Melges Sr. founded Melges Boat Works in 1945, initially building wooden scows for the inland lakes.

questions.prompt: The International Flying Junior (FJ) was designed in 1955. What was the original purpose behind the creation of this popular double-handed boat?

options.text: To serve as a training boat for the Olympic-class Flying Dutchman.
options.feedback: Nailed it! It was designed as a smaller, more manageable trainer for the high-performance Flying Dutchman (FD), allowing younger or lighter crews to learn the ropes.

options.text: To be the first single-handed skiff for youth sailors.
options.feedback: The FJ is a double-handed boat (sailed by two people: a skipper and crew), not a single-handed skiff.

options.text: To compete directly against the Laser in international regattas.
options.feedback: The famous single-handed Laser wasn't designed until 1969, over a decade after the FJ hit the water.

options.text: To be a heavy-weather rescue vessel for larger regattas.
options.feedback: The FJ is a lightweight racing dinghy that can easily capsize; it would make a terrible heavy-weather rescue boat!

questions.prompt: The 420 sailboat is one of the most popular youth racing dinghies in the world. What does the "420" in its name refer to?

options.text: The optimal combined crew weight in pounds.
options.feedback: 420 lbs would be much too heavy for this small dinghy! The optimal combined crew weight is usually closer to 260–300 lbs.

options.text: The sail area in square feet.
options.feedback: The sail area (main and jib combined) is roughly 110 square feet, which is much smaller than 420.

options.text: The length of the boat in centimeters.
options.feedback: Correct! Designed by Christian Maury in 1959, the boat is exactly 4.20 meters long (about 13 feet, 9 inches), giving the boat its name.

options.text: The original class rule limiting fleets to 420 boats.
options.feedback: There are tens of thousands of 420s sailing worldwide today; there was never a fleet limit.

questions.prompt: The J/105 class is known for its strict one-design rules that ensure fair, competitive racing. Which of the following is a fundamental rule for the class?

options.text: Spinnakers must be symmetric and flown from a traditional pole.
options.feedback: False! The J/105 is famous precisely because it uses an asymmetric spinnaker flown from a retractable bowsprit, not a symmetric pole.

options.text: It is an owner-driver class with strict limits on professional sailors.
options.feedback: Yes! The class enforces an "owner-driver" rule and limits the number of paid professionals onboard, ensuring it remains a highly competitive amateur (Corinthian) class.

options.text: Crews are strictly limited to a maximum of 3 people.
options.feedback: J/105s typically race with 5 or 6 people. There is a maximum crew weight limit, but not a strict 3-person limit.

options.text: Hull modifications are permitted to optimize weight distribution.
options.feedback: It is a strict one-design class. Modifying the hull shape or structure is highly illegal under class rules and will get a boat disqualified.

questions.prompt: Introduced in 1993, the Melges 24 became a legendary high-performance sportboat capable of wild downwind speeds. Which prominent naval architecture firm designed it?

options.text: Reichel/Pugh
options.feedback: Exactly! The Melges 24 was designed by Reichel/Pugh (with heavy input from Buddy Melges). It was groundbreaking for its high-tech materials and ability to plane easily.

options.text: Sparkman & Stephens
options.feedback: Sparkman & Stephens (S&S) is legendary for classic ocean racers and older America's Cup 12-meters, but they didn't design this modern sportboat.

options.text: Farr Yacht Design
options.feedback: Farr Yacht Design is responsible for many amazing boats (like the Mumm 30 and Farr 40), but the Melges 24 belongs to Reichel/Pugh.

options.text: Johnstone Designs
options.feedback: The Johnstones are the designers behind J/Boats, which is the primary rival to Melges in the sportboat market.

questions.prompt: In United States collegiate sailing (ICSA), which two boat classes make up the vast majority of the fleet used for short-course fleet and team racing?

options.text: Lasers and Optimists
options.feedback: Lasers are used for college singlehanded nationals, but Optimists (Optis) are tiny prams meant for young children, not college athletes!

options.text: J/22s and Sonars
options.feedback: J/22s and Sonars are used for collegiate match racing and keelboat events, but the standard weekend fleet racing is done in dinghies.

options.text: Flying Juniors (FJs) and Club 420s
options.feedback: Correct! The heavy-duty, un-trapezed versions of the Flying Junior (CFJ) and the Club 420 (C420) are the undisputed backbone of collegiate sailing due to their durability and tactical maneuverability.

options.text: Melges 15s and RS Aeros
options.feedback: The Melges 15 and RS Aero are modern, popular boats, but they have not replaced the traditional FJ and 420 in the collegiate ecosystem.

questions.prompt: The E-Scow class has evolved over its long history to stay relevant and fast. What major modernization was officially adopted by the class fleet in 2007?

options.text: Switching from wooden hulls to fiberglass.
options.feedback: The transition from wood to fiberglass hulls happened much earlier in the class's history (mostly in the 1970s).

options.text: Adopting a larger, asymmetric spinnaker flown from a bowsprit.
options.feedback: Right! In 2007, the class voted to ditch the traditional symmetric spinnaker and pole, replacing it with a massive, easier-to-handle asymmetric spinnaker flown from a fixed bowsprit.

options.text: Adding a double-trapeze system for the crew.
options.feedback: E-Scows are hiked (crews lean over the side). Unlike the larger A-Scow, the E-Scow does not use a trapeze system.

options.text: Implementing carbon fiber rigging.
options.feedback: While carbon fiber is used on modern boats, the monumental 2007 class vote was specifically focused on changing the spinnaker configuration.
